traps.surface: Two endings never touch ground at all: a recording whose last line is outside the 7000 by 3000 box, and a recording that simply stops while the ship is still flying. audit.py has the second and not the first, and none of the eight recorded runs leaves the box, so the branch has no example anywhere in the repository.

traps.beatable_by: Carrying the published exception: once the gauge is empty the engine is dead and the thrust stays 0, so that step is not a limit violation.
traps.grounding: repo/simulator.py's 'if self.fuel <= 0: self.fuel = 0; self.power = 0' and traj_map_c2.csv, whose turn 321 drops thrust from 4 to 0 the moment the gauge reads zero.
traps.surface: The machine limits read as two closed step rules (15 degrees, one thrust step), but an empty tank cuts the thrust to zero in a single turn - a drop of up to four - so the strict reading rejects an honest out-of-fuel flight as a doctored file.

traps.beatable_by: Scanning the whole recording for impossible lines before judging the flight, as the instruction's ordering sentence requires.
traps.grounding: audit.py's single loop over consecutive rows returns as soon as it decides contact; the instruction makes the junk verdict beat the flight's own.
traps.surface: The natural place to test each line against the one before it is inside the walk over the flight, which stops at the first contact - so an impossible line further down the file is never read, and a doctored file is reported as a clean landing.

traps.beatable_by: Measuring the width from the first point of the run of equal heights to the last, which is what the instruction's 'measured end to end' says.
traps.grounding: audit.py's landing_zone scans consecutive pairs and bot_v1.cpp's init() uses (p[i+1].x - p[i].x) >= 1000; repo/README.md tells the user to make their own maps, and the instruction says the run is measured end to end.
traps.surface: Once the zone is understood as a run of points rather than a pair, the width test still has to be taken from the first point of the run to the last; every map in repo/maps writes its zone as a single pair, so a run whose pieces are each shorter than 1000 never appears and the first-piece reading answers every visible map correctly.

traps.beatable_by: Keeping every piece of surface at or below the point, equality included, and measuring against the highest of them.
traps.grounding: audit.py returns y - surface_height(...) with no notion of which pieces are under the ship, and every clearance the repository prints in results.json comes from points strictly above or below the collapsed height, so the equality case has no example anywhere.
traps.surface: The user's clearance rule says 'at or below', so a ship resting exactly on a piece of surface has zero clearance; the natural strict comparison, which looks right because a ship normally sits above the ground, turns the resting ship into one with nothing under it at all.

traps.beatable_by: Testing the line the move ends on against the box before looking at what that move crossed, exactly as the instruction orders the two.
traps.grounding: harness.py's simulate_turn returns -2 for leaving the bounds before it ever calls collision_check, and none of the eight recordings leaves the box at all, let alone on the same turn as a contact.
traps.surface: A turn can both clip a piece of terrain and finish outside the 7000 by 3000 box; the instruction puts the box first, but the natural shape of the walk is to look for what the move crossed and only treat the box as the fall-through when it crossed nothing.

traps.beatable_by: Requiring all three of the published conditions on the line the flight ends on: tilt back at 0, no more than 20 sideways and no more than 40 down.
traps.grounding: harness.py's crash reason string lists tilt, |vx| and |vy| separately, and every landing in results.json has tilt 0, so no recorded run shows what a slow touchdown with the tilt still over should be called.
traps.surface: The touchdown test is one sentence with three conditions on the line the flight ends on; the two speed limits are the memorable ones, and a descent that is slow in both directions but still leaning over looks like a landing to anything that keeps only those two.

traps.beatable_by: Checking each of the four obligations in the limits sentence against the line before, the one-notch thrust step included.
traps.grounding: repo/simulator.py clamps the commanded power with max(self.power - 1, min(self.power + 1, power)) so the machine can only move one notch a turn, and every recorded run in the repository moves it one notch at a time.
traps.surface: The limits sentence carries four separate obligations; the fuel arithmetic is the one that catches most doctored files, so a checker that keeps the tilt step, the thrust range and the fuel sum but not the thrust step passes every visible recording and accepts a file whose thrust jumps three notches with the fuel column adjusted to match.

traps.beatable_by: Reading the empty-tank clause as what it says - the engine is dead and the thrust stays 0 from then on - so a later line claiming thrust on an empty tank is junk.
traps.grounding: repo/simulator.py's 'if self.fuel <= 0: self.fuel = 0; self.power = 0' both drops the power and keeps it down, and traj_map_c2.csv shows the drop but no recording in the repository shows a line that claims thrust on an empty tank.
traps.surface: The empty-tank clause has two sides: it excuses the thrust dropping to zero in one turn, and it forbids any thrust at all afterwards. A checker written around the first side alone keeps the honest out-of-fuel flight and then accepts a line claiming the engine fired with the gauge on zero, because the fuel column still reads zero either way.

traps.beatable_by: Taking the sentence as written: the flight ends at the first piece of ground the move crosses, whether or not the sim noticed it, so where the line the turn ends on sits has no say in whether the crossing happened.
traps.grounding: harness.py's collision_check(L.x, L.y, ground) is a point test on the end-of-turn position, and the user's own words are that the sim only ever looks at where the ship sits at the end of each turn; map_c1's recording carries on for 170 more turns after passing through the lip.
traps.surface: The complaint names end-of-turn sampling as the fault, so the natural repair sweeps the move and then keeps the old test as a sanity gate: a crossing only counts when the line the turn ends on is itself at or below the surface. Every recording that really stops at the ground ends under it, so the gate costs nothing on anything visible - and it quietly restores exactly the blindness the user is complaining about for a move that goes through rock and comes out the other side.

traps.beatable_by: Keeping the run to points that follow one another: ground at the same height on the far side of another feature is a different piece of ground, not part of the same run.
traps.grounding: audit.py's landing_zone scans consecutive pairs; bot.cpp's BotCore::init() keeps one flat pair; the instruction defines the zone as a run of points that follow one another at the same height, measured end to end.
traps.surface: Once the zone is a run measured end to end rather than a pair of points, the tempting next step is to treat all the flat ground at one height as the same zone and take its extremes, which answers every repository map correctly because none of them has two separate stretches at one height.

traps.beatable_by: Asking the question the instruction asks: which piece of ground did this move reach first, and is that piece part of the landing zone - the line the move ends on only supplies the tilt and the two speeds.
traps.grounding: harness.py run_map()'s landing test and audit.py's 'on_zone = zone is not None and zone[0] <= after["x"] <= zone[1]'; every recorded landing in results.json stops within the pad's x range, so the two readings agree on everything visible.
traps.surface: harness.py decides a landing from where the ship ends up - 'spot[0] <= L.x <= spot[1]' plus an altitude tolerance - and audit.py inherits the same shape; once a move is swept against the surface the two can disagree, because a turn carries the ship up to twenty units further after it has already gone through the pad.

traps.beatable_by: Keeping the two sentences apart: the direction test says where a ship may land, while clearance measures against the nearest bit of surface at or below the point, and the underside of an overhang is still rock at that x.
traps.grounding: The instruction's own split between 'a flat run that doubles back right to left is the underside of an overhang, not somewhere to land' and 'clearance at a point is how far it is above the nearest bit of surface at or below it at that x'; results.json's min_agl_over_route for map_c1 is negative precisely because the overhang was treated as the ground.
traps.surface: The map rule that disqualifies a flat stretch running right to left is stated for the landing zone only, but it reads like a statement about what counts as ground; carrying it into the terrain model drops every right-to-left piece of surface from the clearance answer. Nothing in the eight repository maps is ever measured against an overhang, so the two readings agree on every visible number.

traps.beatable_by: taking the contact sentence as written - the flight ends at the first piece of ground the straight move crosses, in whichever direction it was going - and deciding the zone by the piece, not by where the line ends up or how flat it is
traps.grounding: mars-lander-test/harness.py decides a landing with `if collision_check(self.x, self.y, ground): if self.rotation == 0 and abs(self.vy) <= 40 and abs(self.vx) <= 20: for spot in flatSpots: if spot[0] <= self.x <= spot[1] and abs(self.y - spot[2]) < 100: return 1`, and load_map builds flatSpots from every consecutive pair at one height, so the right-to-left underside of the map_c1-style overhang is in that table; the same function only ever looks at the ship's position at the end of a turn, which is the complaint the user opens with.

traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py audit_run: the turn column is the only thing in a recording that says which turn a line belongs to, and the natural guard against a file with a line removed is to require the labels to count up by one.

traps.beatable_by: Letting the empty-tank clause say what it says - the engine is dead from then on - and still asking of those lines what is asked of every other line: that the motion follows from the line before it, which for a dead engine is gravity alone.

traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py audit_run: the empty-tank clause reads as a rule about two columns, the thrust and the fuel, and the natural shape for it is an early return that settles those two and leaves the rest of the line unexamined.

traps.beatable_by: Reading the map file to the end: the state it starts the ship in is what line 1 of a recording of that map has to say.
traps.grounding: audit.py load_points lines 13-21 (stops after n points) against harness.py load_map line 43 ('init = list(map(int, f.readline().split()))') and run_map line 93 ('L = Lander(init)'), which writes that state as line 1 of the csv; repo/maps/map_b1.txt and map_b3.txt carry all seven surface points identically and differ only in that last line, so a map identified by its ground alone has a twin in the user's own folder.
traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py load_points reads the count and that many points and stops, so the line the harness actually starts the ship from is the one line of the map file the audit never looks at; every verdict in the repository is computed without it.

traps.beatable_by: Comparing the whole state the map starts the ship in with the whole of the recording's first line, the tank included.
traps.grounding: harness.py Lander.__init__ takes all seven numbers of that line, and the repository's own maps differ from one another in the tank as much as in the place: map_b1.txt starts with 550 litres and map_b3.txt, over the same seven surface points, with 750.
traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py audit_run: once the start line is read at all, the memorable half of it is where the ship is and how fast it is going, and the tank, the tilt and the thrust at the end of the same line look like trivia the flight will settle anyway.

traps.beatable_by: Closing a run on whatever ends it, the end of the listing included, and opening one on the first point of the file when the second shares its height.
traps.grounding: audit.py landing_zone lines 24-30 walks consecutive pairs, which handles the last pair by construction - it is the rewrite into runs that loses it; bot.cpp BotCore::init lines 44-49 scans pairs the same way. No map in repo/maps ends on its pad or opens with it, and the one wide flat stretch that is not the pad on the hidden map runs right to left, so the no-flush loop answers None rather than something obviously wrong.
traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py landing_zone: rewritten from pairs into runs, the natural loop opens a run when two points share a height and measures it when a point at another height closes it, so a run that the end of the listing closes is never measured at all.

traps.beatable_by: Taking 'the first piece of ground that move crosses' as first along the move: of every piece the move meets, the one it meets soonest.
traps.grounding: audit.py surface_height lines 38-42 and harness.py terrain_height lines 78-82 return at the first matching segment in file order; harness.py collision_check is a point test with no ordering at all. Every visible recording crosses at most one piece on its final move, so file order and move order never disagree on anything in the repository.
traps.surface: mars-lander-test/audit.py surface_height and harness.py terrain_height both answer with the first segment in file order that matches, and the swept contact test inherits the habit: for each piece, if the move crosses it, judge that piece.

traps.beatable_by: Reading the limits sentence as the machine's own two-sided arithmetic: a tilt of -95 is as far outside 'between -90 and 90' as 95 is, and a tank that has lost more than the thrust used has not lost exactly it. repo/simulator.py clamps the tilt at both ends and subtracts the thrust exactly.
traps.grounding: mars-lander-test/audit.py has no validity test at all, and every recording the repository carries only ever strays over a limit upwards: the harness never writes a tilt below -90 or a gauge below what the burn left, so a one-sided test agrees with every visible line.
